title: Welding Basics
summary: Learn the fundamentals of welding: processes such as stick, MIG, TIG and gas, welding safety, machines, current settings and electrode codes, joints, positions and technique, weld defects and inspection, and fabrication and careers. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Beginners, apprentices and workshop workers starting in welding and metal fabrication

body.p: Welding joins metals by melting the edges of the parts, often with added filler metal, so they fuse into one piece as they cool. It is used to build gates, burglar bars, trailers, steel structures, pipelines, ships, vehicles and farm equipment. Skilled welders are in demand across construction, mining, manufacturing and repair.

list: Shielded metal arc welding (SMAW, stick or arc welding): an electric arc between a flux-coated electrode and the work melts both; the flux forms a gas shield and slag. Simple equipment, works outdoors, very common in African workshops.
Gas metal arc welding (GMAW, MIG/MAG): a wire is fed continuously through a gun, shielded by gas; fast and easy to learn, good for thin sheet and production work.
Gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW, TIG): a non-consumable tungsten electrode with separate filler; precise, high quality, used for stainless steel and aluminium.
Oxy-acetylene (gas) welding and cutting: a flame from oxygen and acetylene; widely used for cutting, heating and brazing.

body.p: Related processes include brazing and soldering, which join metals with a filler that melts at a lower temperature without melting the base metal, and plasma cutting.

body.tip: Start with stick welding on mild steel; it teaches arc control that carries over to other processes.

body.p: Welding involves several serious hazards at once, so safety comes first.

list: Arc radiation: ultraviolet and infrared light can burn the eyes (arc eye) and skin within seconds. Always use a welding helmet with the correct shade filter (often around shade 10 to 13 for arc welding) and protect bystanders with screens.
Fumes and gases: welding fumes are harmful, especially from galvanised (zinc-coated) or painted metal. Weld in well-ventilated areas, use extraction, and keep your head out of the plume.
Fire and burns: sparks travel several metres. Remove flammables, keep a fire extinguisher nearby and check for smouldering fires after work.
Electric shock: keep cables, clamps and gloves dry and in good condition, and never weld standing in water.
Gas cylinders: store upright and chained, keep valves closed when not in use, and check for leaks with soapy water, never a flame.

body.p: Wear a helmet, safety glasses under the helmet for grinding and chipping slag, leather gloves, a flame-resistant jacket or overall with no synthetic fabrics, leather boots and, where needed, a respirator.

body.tip: Never weld containers that held fuel or chemicals without proper cleaning; vapours can explode.

body.p: Arc welding machines (transformers, rectifiers or modern inverter machines) supply a controlled current. The main setting is amperage: too low and the arc sticks and the weld sits on top; too high and it spatters, burns through or undercuts.

A common starting rule for stick welding is about 40 A per millimetre of electrode diameter: a 2.5 mm electrode needs roughly 100 A, and a 3.2 mm electrode roughly 128 A, then adjust for position, joint and metal thickness. Always check the electrode packet's recommended range.

list: In codes such as E6013 or E7018 (AWS system), the first two digits give the minimum tensile strength in thousands of psi: E7018 gives 70 000 psi; E6013 gives 60 000 psi.
The third digit shows the welding positions (1 means all positions).
The last digit indicates the coating type and current.
E6013 is easy to use for general mild steel work; E7018 low-hydrogen electrodes are used for stronger, crack-resistant structural welds and must be kept dry.

body.tip: Store electrodes in a dry place; damp electrodes cause porosity and cracking.

list: Butt joint: two plates edge to edge; thicker plates are bevelled for full penetration.
Fillet welds in T-joints and lap joints: the triangular weld in a corner.
Corner and edge joints for frames and sheet metal.

body.p: Welds are made flat (easiest), horizontal, vertical and overhead (hardest). Codes such as 1G and 1F (flat), 2G and 2F (horizontal), 3G and 3F (vertical) and 4G and 4F (overhead) are used in welder qualification tests.

list: Prepare: clean rust, paint and oil; fit up parts with the right gap; tack weld to hold them.
Arc length: about the same as the electrode core diameter.
Angle: tilt the electrode slightly in the direction of travel.
Travel speed: steady; too fast gives a thin, weak bead, too slow a wide, heavy one.
Chip off slag and brush between runs on multi-pass welds.

body.p: Fillet weld size is set by the leg length; a common rule of thumb is a throat of about 0.7 times the leg, so a 6 mm leg gives about a 4.2 mm throat.

body.tip: Practise straight beads on scrap plate until they are even before attempting joints.

list: Porosity: gas holes, often from damp electrodes, dirty metal or wind blowing away shielding gas.
Slag inclusions: slag trapped in the weld from poor cleaning between runs.
Undercut: a groove melted into the base metal at the weld edge, often from too much current or a long arc.
Lack of fusion or penetration: the weld does not properly bond, from too little heat or poor joint preparation.
Cracks: the most serious defect, from rapid cooling, high carbon steels, hydrogen or restraint.
Distortion: parts bend as hot metal shrinks; tacking, balanced welding sequences and clamping help.

body.p: Heat input affects strength and distortion. It can be estimated as volts x amps x 60 / travel speed (mm per minute) / 1000, in kJ/mm. At 24 V, 150 A and 200 mm/min this is about 1.08 kJ/mm; travelling at 300 mm/min reduces it to 0.72 kJ/mm.

Visual inspection is the first check. Other methods include dye penetrant and magnetic particle tests for surface cracks, and ultrasonic or radiographic testing for internal defects. Bend tests on sample welds are used to qualify welders.

body.tip: Look at every weld you make, judge it honestly, and change one setting at a time to improve.

body.p: Fabrication turns drawings into metal products. Steps include reading the drawing, measuring and marking out, cutting, bending, fitting, tacking, welding, grinding and finishing with primer and paint to prevent rust.

list: Cutting: angle grinders with cutting discs, hacksaws, oxy-fuel cutting for thick steel and plasma cutters for clean, fast cuts.
Grinding: wear eye and face protection, and check that the disc speed rating matches the grinder.
Measuring: work to drawings, check squareness with diagonals, and allow for distortion.
Estimating: for a gate frame of 6 m of square tube at 3 joints per metre, plan for about 18 weld joints and the electrodes and time they need.

body.p: Welders and boilermakers train through apprenticeships, technical colleges and trade tests, and certify to codes for specific positions and processes. Opportunities include construction, mining, oil and gas, shipbuilding, agriculture and self-employment making gates, burglar bars, furniture and trailers.

body.tip: Certification in pipe welding and in all positions significantly increases pay and job prospects.
